categories.title: Folding too easily to flop bets
categories.fix: Before you fold to a flop bet, count your outs and compare your chance to win with the price of the call, because one small bet often buys a cheap look at the turn.
categories.justification: A flop bet is a small bet into a pot already holding several bets, so the price is low and pairs and draws often have the equity to call (pot-odds-call, implied-odds-call).

categories.title: Calling flop bets without the odds
categories.fix: Call a flop bet only when your chance to win, counting your outs, is at least the price of the call, and raise instead when you are well ahead of the hands that would call a raise.
categories.justification: A call is graded against the pot-odds price and against the value-raise rule, so calls go wrong both when the hand is too weak and when it is strong enough to raise.

categories.title: Raising the flop with hands that are not ahead
categories.fix: Raise a flop bet only when your hand beats most of the hands that will call the raise, and just call with draws and medium hands that need to improve.
categories.justification: The value-raise rule asks for more than 65% equity against the hands that would call a raise, so a hand below that bar should just call or fold by the pot-odds and implied-odds rules (value-raise, pot-odds-call, implied-odds-call).

categories.title: Checking the flop with hands that should bet
categories.fix: When the flop is checked to you and your hand beats most of the hands that would call, bet so that weaker hands pay you now.
categories.justification: The value-bet rule bets when the hero is ahead of the calling range; checking those hands gives up a bet the opponents would have paid.

categories.title: Betting the flop into better hands
categories.fix: Bet the flop only when most of the hands that would call are worse than yours, and check the rest, because a check costs nothing now and you see the turn for free if no one bets after you.
categories.justification: A bet earns only from worse hands that pay it; when the hands that call are mostly better, the check-free rule is the better play.

categories.title: Folding too often on the turn
categories.fix: Before you fold to a turn bet, compare your chance to win with the price of the call plus the river bet that usually follows, and call whenever your chance is at least that price.
categories.justification: A turn call is priced with the river big bet the hero will likely face, and the call is right when equity is at least that price, or a little less for a draw that wins more bets when it hits (pot-odds-call, implied-odds-call).

categories.title: Calling too often on the turn
categories.fix: The turn bet is twice the size of a flop bet, so call it only with a made hand that is often best or a draw whose outs pay for the price.
categories.justification: A draw has only one card to come on the turn instead of two, so its equity drops while the price now counts the likely river big bet too, and calls that were fine on the flop can lose on the turn (pot-odds-call, pot-odds-fold).

categories.title: Raising the turn without a strong hand
categories.fix: Raise a turn bet only with a hand that beats most of the hands that will call, because a raise at the big-bet level costs twice as much when you are behind.
categories.justification: The value-raise rule needs more than 65% equity against the hands that would call a raise, and the cost of being wrong doubles on the turn (value-raise).

categories.title: Checking the turn with hands that should bet
categories.fix: When the turn is checked to you with a hand that beats most of the hands that would call, bet the big bet instead of giving draws a free card.
categories.justification: The value-bet rule bets when ahead of the calling range; a check on the turn also lets drawing hands see the river for nothing.

categories.title: Betting the turn without enough hand
categories.fix: Bet the turn only when your hand is ahead of most of the hands that would call, since a big bet into better hands loses twice what it did on the flop.
categories.justification: A turn bet is a big bet; betting into a calling range that is mostly ahead loses a full big bet each time it is called.

categories.title: Folding the river when the pot pays you to call
categories.fix: On the river the pot is usually many times the bet, so call with any hand that wins often enough to cover the price instead of folding it.
categories.justification: With the pot many big bets deep, the required equity for a river call is low, so folding hands that win that often throws away value (pot-odds-call).

categories.title: Calling the river with hands that rarely win
categories.fix: Call a river bet only when your hand wins at least as often as the price of the call demands, because no more cards can come to help you.
categories.justification: On the river there are no outs left, so the call is right only when current equity meets the pot-odds price (pot-odds-call, pot-odds-fold).

categories.title: Raising the river with hands that only beat bluffs
categories.fix: Raise the river only when most of the hands that will call your raise are worse than yours.
categories.justification: On the river a raise is only for value: worse hands fold to it and better hands call or re-raise unless the hero is ahead of the calling range (value-raise).

categories.title: Checking the river with hands worth a bet
categories.fix: When the river is checked to you with a hand that beats most of the hands that would call, bet it, because a check gives up the last chance to be paid.
categories.justification: The value-bet rule bets when ahead of the calling range, and the river is the last chance to collect that bet.

categories.title: Betting the river into better hands
categories.fix: Bet the river only when most of the hands that would call are worse than yours, and check medium hands that nothing worse will pay.
categories.justification: On the river worse hands fold and better hands call, so a bet with a medium hand gains little and loses a big bet against the hands that pay it.

categories.title: Folding strong hands from early position
categories.fix: From early position, open-raise the strong hands the chart plays instead of folding them, because they stay profitable even with many players left to act.
categories.justification: The early-position charts still open premium pairs, big aces and strong broadway hands, so folding those hands gives up a profitable open.

categories.title: Opening too many hands from early position
categories.fix: From early position, open-raise only the tight range on the chart, because with many players still to act a strong hand often wakes up behind you.
categories.justification: With the most players left to act, the early-position chart range is the narrowest; hands outside it are too often dominated by a caller or re-raiser.

categories.title: Calling too often from early position
categories.fix: From early position, raise or fold rather than limp, and call a raise only with the few hands the chart calls with.
categories.justification: The charts do not limp from early position and call raises with few hands, because players still to act can raise behind and you will often play the pot out of position.

categories.title: Re-raising too loosely from early position
categories.fix: Re-raise from early position only with hands that are well ahead of the raiser's range, since the players behind you can still re-raise again.
categories.justification: The re-raise rows of the charts hold only hands that beat the raiser's range; with players left to act, a weaker re-raise risks a cap from a stronger hand.

categories.title: Folding playable hands from middle position
categories.fix: From middle position, open-raise the hands the chart opens, because fewer players are left to act and a wider range now wins.
categories.justification: The middle-position chart range is wider than the early one, so folding hands inside it gives up opens the chart rates as profitable.

categories.title: Opening too many hands from middle position
categories.fix: From middle position, open-raise only the chart's middle range, which is wider than early position but still leaves out weak aces and small offsuit hands.
categories.justification: Several players are still to act behind a middle-position open, so hands outside the chart range are too often behind the hands that continue.

categories.title: Calling too often from middle position
categories.fix: From middle position, raise the hands worth playing in an unopened pot and call a raise only with hands that play well against the raiser's range.
categories.justification: The charts prefer raising to limping when the pot is unopened and call raises only with hands that do well after the flop against the raiser.

categories.title: Re-raising too loosely from middle position
categories.fix: Re-raise from middle position only with hands that beat most of the raiser's range, and fold or call with the rest.
categories.justification: The re-raise rows of the charts hold only hands ahead of the raiser's range; weaker re-raises build a pot while behind.

categories.title: Folding too much from late position
categories.fix: From the cutoff and button, open-raise the wide range the chart allows, because only the blinds are left to act and you will have position after the flop.
categories.justification: The late-position charts open the widest range since only the blinds remain and the opener acts last after the flop, so folding those hands gives up easy profit.

categories.title: Opening too many hands from late position
categories.fix: Even on the cutoff and button, open-raise only the chart's late range and fold the weakest hands that rarely win against the blinds.
categories.justification: The late range is wide but not every hand; the weakest hands lose more when the blinds defend than they win when the blinds fold.

categories.title: Calling too often from late position
categories.fix: From late position, raise rather than limp when the pot is unopened, and call a raise only with hands that play well after the flop.
categories.justification: The charts raise rather than limp from late position to win the blinds or play a heads-up pot in position, and call raises only with hands that do well after the flop.

categories.title: Re-raising too loosely from late position
categories.fix: From late position, re-raise only with hands that beat most of the raiser's range, keeping in mind that an early raiser holds stronger hands.
categories.justification: The charts re-raise against the raiser's range for that seat, and an early-position raiser's range is strong, so a loose re-raise is often behind.

categories.title: Folding too often from the blinds
categories.fix: In the blinds you already have chips in the pot, so defend the hands the chart defends instead of folding them to a single raise.
categories.justification: The blind-defence rows of the charts account for the chips already posted, which lower the price of a call, so folding those hands gives up value.

categories.title: Raising too loosely from the blinds
categories.fix: From the blinds, raise an unopened or limped pot only with hands strong enough to play out of position on every later street.
categories.justification: A blind acts first on every street after the flop, so the charts raise from the blinds with fewer hands than from late position.

categories.title: Calling too often from the blinds
categories.fix: From the blinds, complete or call only with hands that can win enough after the flop to make up for acting first on every street.
categories.justification: Calls from the blinds are cheap but are played out of position, so the charts call only with hands that keep enough value after the flop.

categories.title: Re-raising too loosely from the blinds
categories.fix: From the blinds, re-raise only with hands that are well ahead of the raiser's range, because you will be out of position for the rest of the hand.
categories.justification: The re-raise rows of the blind-defence charts hold only hands ahead of the raiser's range, since being out of position makes marginal re-raises lose.
